answer.text: would have been blocked by the standing rules of the prize itself
answer.line: Paragraph 10: no prize goes to anyone who died before being nominated. Franklin died in 1958; the prize came in 1962.

steps: Find the 1962 prize: paragraph 10, sentence 6 states two rules.
One rule settles it. A prize "is not given to anyone who died before being nominated," and sentence 5 says she died in April 1958.
Join the two: rule plus date. Whatever the committee wished, the prize's own rules stood in the way, so the question "was never put."

choices.text: would have had to remove Wilkins from the list to make room for her
choices.note: The three-person cap is real, but she had died before nomination, so making room on the list would not have helped.

choices.text: would have been blocked by the standing rules of the prize itself
choices.note: Sentence 6 gives the rules; sentence 5 gives the date that trips them.

choices.text: would have needed the consent of Watson and Crick to do so
choices.note: No one's consent appears anywhere. The passage names only the prize's own rules.

choices.text: would have waited until her notebooks had been examined by Klug
choices.note: Klug's reading of her notebooks is in paragraph 11, part of the later debate over credit. It is not a prize rule.

choices.text: would have awarded the prize in chemistry instead of in medicine
choices.note: A chemistry prize sounds like a way in for a trained chemist, but sentence 6 names the field only to report the award. The rules it states hold for any prize.

lockIt: Inference: join a stated rule to a stated fact, and add nothing the passage does not give you.
